FinPolNomics GREEN FINANCE with FinPolNomics ANALYTICA · Regulatory Intelligence Series 2026

Nigeria's insurance reform, decoded for every seat at the table.

An interactive briefing on the Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025 (NIIRA), the Insurance Regulatory Commission Bill 2025 and the insurance-relevant provisions of the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation Act 2023, with calculators, simulations, games and a certified quiz.

NIIRA 2025 repealed five Acts in one stroke (s.229).

Conversation starters for the room

  • If your employer has no group life policy and a colleague dies tomorrow, who pays, and how much? (s.68(9))
  • Should a broker that holds client premiums for 45 days lose its commission, its licence, or both? (s.61)
  • Why did the law abolish the old rule that let an insurer avoid a marine policy for any lack of utmost good faith? (s.138)
  • Is a 0.25% levy enough to build a policyholder protection fund worth 10% of industry exposure? (s.212)

Two safety nets compared: NDIC deposit insurance funds and the NIIRA Policyholders Protection Fund

FeatureNDIC deposit insurance fundsNIIRA Insurance Policyholders Protection Fund
Legal basisNDIC Act s.17 (five funds by institution type)NIIRA s.212
Who is protectedDepositors of licensed deposit-taking institutions (s.21, s.22)Policyholders with admitted but unpaid claims of insolvent or delicensed insurers (s.212(2))
FundingAnnual risk-based premiums on total deposits (s.23(2)); special contributions up to 200% of annual premium (s.23(7))0.25% of gross premium income of every insurer and reinsurer, plus 0.25% of the Security and Insurance Development Fund balance (s.212(1)); additional calls (s.212(7))
Target sizeMinimum target fund size and ratio set by the NDIC Board (s.17(4), (5))At least 10% of prior-year total industry exposure, or an amount the Commission considers adequate (s.212(15))
How money goes outDirect payment of insured deposits; assistance capped at 10% of a fund (s.17(7))Loans for distress resolution and unpaid claims, repayable or a first-line charge in liquidation (s.212(6))
Coverage limitStatutory ₦500,000 (₦200,000 for microfinance banks) in s.25(1); raised under s.25(2) in May 2024 to ₦5m for deposit money banks and ₦2m for MFBs, PMBs and PSBsNo limit in the Act; to be set in Commission guidelines (s.212(11))
Payout timelineWithin 30 days of becoming liquidator (s.28(1))Not specified in the Act
GovernanceNDIC Board chaired by the Permanent Secretary, Finance (s.7)Committee: chair appointed by the Commission, two Commission and two industry representatives, fund manager as secretary (s.212(5))
Ring-fencingHeld in trust per category of institution (s.17(7))Managed independently and never co-mingled with Commission funds (s.212(4))
Priority in failureDeposit liabilities rank ahead of all other liabilities (s.72)Policyholders rank immediately after liquidation fees (s.110(5))

Statutory deposit calculator (s.16)

New entrants deposit 50% of the minimum capital with the CBN; 80% of that is returned with interest within 60 days of registration. Existing insurers keep 10% on deposit.

%
Illustrative. Income is paid bi-annually (s.16(4)).

What counts, and what does not

For an existing company the minimum capital comprises admissible assets less liabilities (less own shares), approved subordinated liabilities and other prescribed instruments (s.15(5)). A new company may hold it in Government bonds, treasury bills, cash and cash equivalents (s.15(4)).

Is there valid cover? (s.60)

Answer the questions in order.

The rule in brief. No cover without advance premium (s.60(1)). Premium paid to a licensed broker counts as paid to the insurer (s.60(2)). Exceptions: third-party covers under compulsory insurance (s.60(4)) and reinsurance contracts (s.60(5)). Breach: up to twice the premium (s.60(3)).
  • Premium loading in any form is prohibited (s.63(3)).
  • Agents may not collect premium at all (s.38(2)).
  • Brokers remit within 20 working days or 30 calendar days (s.61(1)).

Broker premium remittance calculator (s.61)

A broker must pay the insurer within 20 working days or 30 calendar days of receipt of premium, the effective date or the due date of cover, whichever is later. Late remittance attracts interest at 2% above the CBN minimum rediscount rate and a penalty.

₦m

Claims delay cost calculator (s.210)

Admitted claims must be settled within 60 days of notification. Special risk claims must be admitted or denied within 60 days and settled within 60 days of the discharge voucher. Delay attracts a ₦500,000 penalty plus monthly compound interest at the prevailing bank rate.

Retirement life annuity exemption (s.36)

Amounts payable as retirement life annuity, including interest, dividends, profits and investments, are not subject to tax and levies in any form.

₦m
%
Illustrative.
Interpretive point for tax advisers. NIIRA s.21(3) says insurance reserves and other business expenses are "fully deductible for tax purposes", and s.230(2) gives NIIRA priority over inconsistent laws where they relate to insurance business. The Nigeria Tax Act 2025, s.61, sets its own computation rules for unexpired risks, outstanding claims and life reserves. Where the two differ, the interaction should be confirmed with the Nigeria Revenue Service and professional advisers before filing positions are taken.

Professional caveat

This dashboard is an independent educational and analytical publication of FinPolNomics GREEN FINANCE and FinPolNomics ANALYTICA. It summarises the Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025 (as published in the Federal Government Gazette No. 146, Vol. 112), the Insurance Regulatory Commission Bill 2025 (uploaded text, which may differ from any version passed or assented) and selected provisions of the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation Act 2023.

It is not legal, tax, actuarial, investment or accounting advice, and it does not create a professional relationship. Summaries are simplified; the statutory text, regulations, circulars and guidelines issued by the Commission, NDIC, the CBN and the Nigeria Revenue Service prevail. Readers should obtain advice from qualified professionals before acting.

Calculators, simulators and charts use illustrative assumptions, including interest rates, capital charges, premium rates, tax rates, GDP and exposure proxies. They are teaching tools and are not regulatory computations. Industry statistics are drawn from public reports cited in the Sources panel and are subject to revision.

The status of the IRC Bill, the recapitalisation outcome and other facts are stated as at 8 October 2026. Laws and regulatory positions change; verify currency before reliance.

Views are those of the curator in a professional and personal capacity and do not represent the positions of AOS Orwell Limited, Sahara Group, NECA, NAICOM, NDIC, the Nigerian Insurers Association, the Nigerian Actuarial Society or any other institution. Logos are shown for identification only.

Quiz certificates acknowledge completion of an online self-assessment. They are not a professional qualification, licence or continuing professional development credit unless a professional body confirms otherwise.
